blocks.text: I can explain how animals can be grouped using observable characteristics.
Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: To classify is to sort into groups.
To identify something is to be able to name it correctly.
A vertebrate is an animal with an internal skeleton, including a spine.
Animals that do not have bones, including a spine, on the inside of their bodies are invertebrates.
Classification keys are diagrams which help us sort things into different groups.

blocks.text: There are millions of species of animals living on planet Earth, and scientists are discovering new ones all the time.
Scientists {classify}, or group, animals to make it easier to identify, name and learn more about them.

Scientists who specialise in identifying and classifying animals are called **taxonomists**. When a new animal is discovered, taxonomists look at the similarities and differences between it and other animals to decide which group it belongs in.
One way taxonomists classify animals is by sorting them into two main groups.

items.title: {Vertebrates}
items.sub: Have a spine (or backbone) and an internal skeleton.

items.title: {Invertebrates}
items.sub: Do not have a spine or internal skeleton.

blocks.label: Think about an X-ray
blocks.text: An X-ray shows bones. Humans are vertebrates. An X-ray of an invertebrate will show no bones.
If invertebrates don’t have skeletons, how are their bodies supported and their organs protected?

items.def: A hard outer covering that protects the body of some invertebrates. As the animal grows, it moults its exoskeleton, and its fresh outer layer hardens to form a new, larger exoskeleton.
A body filled with fluid that supports the body and helps some invertebrates to move. A slug and an octopus have hydrostatic skeletons.

blocks.text: Some animals can be difficult to classify because of the way they look. Tap to find out about each pair.

blocks.label: Tortoise and crab
blocks.text: Both have hard shells on their backs. The tortoise is a reptile. It has a spine and an internal skeleton, so it is a **vertebrate**. The crab’s shell is part of its exoskeleton. It has no internal skeleton, so it is an **invertebrate**.

blocks.label: Earthworm and snake
blocks.text: Both are very bendy and have no arms or legs. The snake is a reptile. It has a spine and an internal skeleton, so it is a **vertebrate**. The earthworm has no internal skeleton, so it is an **invertebrate**.

blocks.q: Put each animal in the right group.

blocks.text: Vertebrates can be divided further into these groups.

blocks.q: Put each animal in its vertebrate group.
Now these ones: amphibian or reptile?

blocks.text: Invertebrates can be classified into further groups, including these four.

items.title: Insects
items.sub: Six legs, a body divided into three segments and a pair of antennae. Beetles, bees, butterflies, ants.

items.title: Arachnids
items.sub: Eight legs and a body divided into two sections. Spiders, harvestmen, scorpions, ticks.

items.title: Crustaceans
items.sub: A hard exoskeleton and two pairs of antennae. Crabs, lobsters, shrimp, barnacles.

items.title: Molluscs
items.sub: A very soft body and hydrostatic skeletons. Some also have shells. Slugs, snails, squid, octopuses.

blocks.q: Match each invertebrate group to what it is like.

pairs.b: six legs and a body divided into three segments
eight legs and a body in two sections
a hard exoskeleton and two pairs of antennae
a very soft body and hydrostatic skeletons

blocks.q: Now sort these invertebrates into their groups.

blocks.text: We can use classification keys to help us identify unfamiliar animals. A key has a series of yes / no questions about the observable characteristics of living things. Each question leads you to a new question until you identify the living thing.

items: Does it have wings? Yes: Does it have feathers? Yes: robin. No: butterfly.
Does it have wings? No: Does it have a shell? Yes: snail. No: slug.

blocks.text: There are always just two answers to a question in a key: {yes} or {no}.

blocks.q: Which of these could NOT be a question in a classification key?
blocks.why: Questions in a classification key must always be answered with either yes or no. “What colour is it?” has many possible answers.

blocks.text: Alex made a key. Does the animal have wings? If yes: does it have antennae? Yes = red admiral butterfly, no = kingfisher. If no: does it have an exoskeleton? Yes = red ghost crab, no = octopus.

blocks.q: Which animal does the key give for each set of answers?

blocks.text: We can use what we know about similarities and differences to create a classification key. Sofia found a bee, a spider, a snail, an ant and a slug in the school grounds.
First, ask a yes / no question that divides the animals into two groups. Keep asking questions until there is only one animal left at the end of each branch.

blocks.label: Sofia’s key
blocks.text: Does it have legs? Yes: bee, spider, ant. No: snail, slug. For the no branch she asks: does it have a shell? Yes: snail. No: slug. For the yes branch she asks: does it have wings? Yes: bee. No: spider, ant, so she asks: is the body divided into two sections? Yes: spider. No: ant.

blocks.q: Sofia wants to split the snail and the slug. Which question works?
options: How many legs does it have?
blocks.why: The snail has a shell and the slug does not, and it is a yes / no question.

items: Scientists classify animals to make it easier to identify, name and learn about them.
Animals can be classified by looking at similarities and differences in their observable characteristics.
Animals can be divided into vertebrates and invertebrates, then grouped again within these categories.
We can create classification keys for animals by asking a series of yes / no questions about their observable characteristics.

flashcards.front: What do we do when we classify animals?

flashcards.back: To make it easier to identify, name and learn more about them.

flashcards.front: What are scientists who specialise in identifying and classifying animals called?

flashcards.back: An animal with an internal skeleton, including a spine (or backbone).
An animal that does not have bones, including a spine, on the inside of its body.
A hard outer covering that protects the body of some invertebrates. The animal moults it as it grows, and a new, larger one hardens.

A body filled with fluid that supports the body and helps an invertebrate to move.

Examples: a slug and an octopus.

flashcards.front: Name the five groups of vertebrates in this lesson.
flashcards.back: Mammals, birds, fish, amphibians and reptiles.

Six legs, a body divided into three segments and a pair of antennae.

Examples: beetles, bees, butterflies, ants.

Eight legs and a body divided into two sections.

Examples: spiders, harvestmen, scorpions, ticks.

A hard exoskeleton and two pairs of antennae.

Examples: crabs, lobsters, shrimp, barnacles.

A very soft body and hydrostatic skeletons. Some also have shells.

Examples: slugs, snails, squid, octopuses.

flashcards.front: What kind of questions are used in a classification key?
flashcards.back: Yes / no questions about observable characteristics. Each question leads to a new question until you identify the living thing.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: How and why we group animals
worksheet.instructions: Answer each question with a word, a number or a short phrase, using what you learned in the lesson.

questions.prompt: Animals that have a spine are called what? (one word)
questions.explanation: A vertebrate is an animal with an internal skeleton, including a spine.

questions.prompt: Is a lobster a vertebrate or an invertebrate?
questions.explanation: Its hard covering is an exoskeleton. It has no spine or internal skeleton.

questions.prompt: Is an eel a vertebrate or an invertebrate?
questions.explanation: An eel is a fish, so it is a vertebrate with a spine, even though it is very bendy.

questions.prompt: What is the name for the hard outer covering that protects the body of some invertebrates?
questions.explanation: A hard outer covering on the outside of the body is an exoskeleton.

questions.prompt: What are scientists who specialise in identifying and classifying animals called?
Which group of invertebrates has eight legs and a body divided into two sections?
questions.explanation: Arachnids, such as spiders and scorpions, have eight legs and a body in two sections.

questions.prompt: Which group of invertebrates has a very soft body and hydrostatic skeletons, and includes slugs and snails?
questions.explanation: Molluscs have a very soft body and hydrostatic skeletons. Some also have shells.

questions.prompt: How many legs does an insect have?
questions.explanation: Insects have six legs, a body divided into three segments and a pair of antennae.

questions.prompt: A frog, a newt and an axolotl all belong to which group of vertebrates?
questions.explanation: Newts, frogs and axolotls are amphibians.

questions.prompt: Which group of invertebrates has a hard exoskeleton and two pairs of antennae, and includes crabs and lobsters?
questions.explanation: Crustaceans have a hard exoskeleton and two pairs of antennae.
